Collateral

/kuh-LAT-er-ul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Collateral means secondary or incidental, especially describing an unintended side effect of a primary action.

Collateral means secondary or incidental, especially describing an unintended side effect of a primary action. Closing the highway for repairs had the collateral effect of doubling traffic on the quiet streets nearby.

Worked Example

The city sprayed its parks to control an invasive beetle, and the treatment worked exactly as planned. But within weeks, gardeners noticed that the spraying had also thinned the population of harmless fireflies. No one had set out to harm them; their decline was collateral damage from a campaign aimed at a completely different insect. The parks department revised its methods the following season to protect them.

The fireflies' decline was an unintended side effect of an action aimed at something else entirely, which is what collateral describes.

How Collateral Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

incidental

incidental: happening as a minor, unplanned accompaniment

secondary

secondary: of lesser importance than the main thing

Antonyms

primary

primary: first in importance; the main aim

intended

intended: planned as the goal from the start

How Strong Is It? — ancillary → collateral → inadvertent

ancillary vs. collateral

ancillary vs. collateral: An ancillary effect is a supporting result that a plan often counts on, while a collateral effect sits outside the plan's aim entirely.

inadvertent vs. collateral

inadvertent vs. collateral: A collateral effect is unintended but often foreseeable, while an inadvertent one happens through pure oversight, with no one seeing it coming at all.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of collateral.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — col-

Prefix — col-: a form of com-, meaning together or alongside

Root — later

Root — later: from Latin latus, lateris, side

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: characteristic of, pertaining to, having the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Collateral combines col-, a form of the Latin prefix com- meaning 'together or alongside,' with the root latus, 'side,' and the suffix -al, 'characteristic of.' Something collateral is literally 'characteristic of being alongside': it runs at the side of the main action rather than at its center, which is why an unintended side effect is a collateral effect.

Use the root in a new word: bilateral

Use the root in a new word: bilateral: The two countries signed a bilateral agreement, literally a two-sided one, built on the same Latin root latus, 'side.'

Root Check

Word Choice

formal, policy/analytical register

Collateral describes what happens off to the side of an action's real aim (collateral damage, a collateral benefit). In banking, the related noun collateral names property pledged alongside a loan, standing at the lender's side as security; the shared idea in both senses is 'at the side.' Do not confuse the adjective with tangential, which judges how a remark relates to a topic of discussion rather than what an action accidentally causes.
